extracted.intended_audience: general newspaper readers interested in U.S. labor, housing and postwar public policy
extracted.subtask_description: AP-style news coverage of U.S. federal labor-policy proposals, fact‑finding boards, union-management disputes, and housing/price-control measures in the immediate postwar period. Includes procedural details, policy proposals, and administrative directives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-finding board duration and strike ban
rubrics_metrics.description: The President had proposed twenty days for the fact-finding, with strikes banned five days before the board’s inquiry and five days after its conclusion; the fact‑finding period could be extended only if absolutely necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes the 20-day limit and the five‑day pre/post prohibition; a reporter said period could be extended if the board thought it justified, but the President/administration expressed skepticism about broad extension and said extension only if 'absolutely necessary.' This is presented as a legislative/design constraint intended to limit delays while fact‑finders work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-finding boards should not interfere with collective bargaining
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointment of fact-finders 'is not intended to interfere in any way with the parties’ collective bargaining which is now in process,' and it was hoped the parties would settle differences by agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The White House/President framed fact‑finding as investigatory and complementary to bargaining, and union leaders were urged to 'cooperate' and 'place before the committee all the facts and figures' to facilitate resolution. Critics argued inquiries starting while negotiations are in progress might impede settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension/independence of individual action during fact-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: A provision allowing individual members 'acting independently' to strike was included while organized strikes would be banned during fact‑finding; critics called this 'window dressing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics (AFL) said such a clause was inserted to try to preserve constitutionality but would amount to little protection for labor because organized strikes would still be banned while boards work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government injunctions, criminal contempt and civil damages in proposed strike legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal would 'reestablish' government by injunction, subjecting violators to criminal contempt charges and to imprisonment; civil damage suits would be authorized and encouraged against the union, officers as individuals, and individual members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This passage lists the punitive/legal mechanisms the proposed legislation would revive—criminal contempt, imprisonment, and civil suits—presented as major consequences of the bill and a focus of labor opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional and labor-rights objections to strike‑curbing proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents argued the proposal 'invades the right to strike' and 'clearly imposes involuntary servitude on workers,' and that constitutional rights (freedom of speech, assembly) would be threatened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records labor leaders' legal and constitutional criticisms (e.g., Green, AFL), framing these as central political and legal objections that could shape debate and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company-security/penalty provisions in labor contracts (union vs. employer approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ford proposed the union assume financial responsibility for unauthorized work stoppages (e.g., $5-a-day penalty from the union for each worker who engages in an unauthorized walkout); the union proposed disciplining leaders/instigators and fining participants ($1 a day first offense, $2 for the second).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece contrasts employer and union security/penalty proposals and notes legal doubts as to the right to penalize; shows how different security schemes assign liability either to the union as a body or to individual workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Labor Board vacation-pay eligibility criteria (Higgins Industries order)
rubrics_metrics.description: The War Labor Board directed Higgins Industries to pay employees with one year or more of service five days' vacation with pay (retroactive to Jan. 1) if they had worked not less than 1,500 straight‑time hours prior to June 1; ten days' vacation with pay for employees who had worked 1,500 straight‑time hours during each of the three years preceding June 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concrete administrative eligibility rule specifying service and hours thresholds and retroactivity—used here as an example of WLB enforcement of employee benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'no‑strike' contract clauses and reopening for national wage policy change
rubrics_metrics.description: The United Steelworkers contended contract clauses that appear to prohibit strikes allow reopening the contract for a general wage increase 'upon a change in national wage policy'; the War Labor Board in a unanimous resolution recognized the union is free to bargain with respect to a general wage increase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a legal/interpretive standard governing whether a union's no‑strike pledge bars a national strike when national wage policy changes; presented as union argument and WLB backing, relevant to legality of planned strikes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for setting price ceilings on new houses
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patman bill (as described) would determine ceilings on new houses 'on the basis of actual construction costs, plus the fair market value of the land and the generally prevailing contractors’ margin for comparable units in 1941.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplies the formulaic standard the administration favored for calculating ceilings on new housing; the White House and Reconversion director called such authority essential to avert 'sky-rocketing' prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for setting price ceilings on existing homes
rubrics_metrics.description: On an existing home, the ceiling would be 'the price at which it is first sold after enactment of the bill.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an administratively simple rule (first‑sale price) for capping prices of existing homes upon legislative enactment; the article notes ceilings would be limited to areas where a Federal housing director found it necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priorities for building materials and veterans preference
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed priorities program would establish priorities on building materials, earmarking about 50 percent of construction supplies for single or multiple dwelling housing units costing $10,000 or less per unit, and would set up preferences for veterans in purchase or rental of such housing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administration actions would reinstate a wartime‑style priorities system under the Second War Powers Act; priorities would be geographically adjusted and make veterans preferred recipients of materials and housing vacancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑point presidential housing program
rubrics_metrics.description: The President's three‑point program called for: (1) Speedy release of government‑owned surplus housing units and building materials for veterans; (2) A regulation establishing priorities on building materials (targeting dwellings costing $10,000 or less); (3) Ceiling prices on old and new housing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames these three points as the core immediate administrative steps requested/endorsed by the President to meet the acute housing emergency while longer‑term legislation is pursued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six objectives of the War Mobilization and Reconversion housing program
rubrics_metrics.description: The WM&R six objectives: (1) increase supply of building materials; (2) strengthen inventory controls to prevent hoarding; (3) strengthen price controls over building materials; (4) discourage unsound lending practices and speculation; (5) enlist industry support in increasing production and fighting inflation; (6) provide advisory service on home values to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as coordinated executive-agency measures to meet emergency housing needs—tools include price controls, allocations/priority, manpower recruitment, and industry coordination; examples of production increases (pipe, bricks, gypsum) are given as outcomes.
